name: Entry-level jobs
question: How is generative AI changing entry-level hiring, employment, earnings, and the routes through which people gain experience?
synthesis: This bounded scoping scan finds adverse early-career hiring and earnings associations in some US and online-platform samples, alongside limited or null average effects in Danish, Finnish, and Norwegian evidence. Task-level productivity gains, especially for less-experienced workers, do not establish that employers will hire more entrants or pass gains into pay. Exposure measures, age bands, vacancies, worker earnings, and employment stocks answer different questions; neither the adverse nor the null findings establish an economy-wide causal effect of generative AI.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
sources.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
sources.design: Observational balanced-firm ADP payroll panel; occupation-exposure and age comparisons with controls.
sources.population: Full-time, positive-earnings, occupation-coded ADP workers under 70; ages 22-25 compared with older workers and less-exposed peers.
sources.duration: January 2021-June 2026; extended pretrend panel from January 2018. Revision August 12, 2026; original release August 2025.
sources.measure: Employment growth, hires, separations, and base compensation by exposure and age.
sources.finding: From November 2022 to June 2026, employment of ages 22-25 in the top two exposure quintiles was 19% below the level implied by bottom-three-quintile growth. Hiring drove the gap; experienced workers had no comparable gap.
sources.limitations: Descriptive association, not 19% of youth jobs lost to AI. Education controls attenuate estimates, pretrends differ, and ADP is not nationally representative.
sources.locator: Abstract; Sections 1.1, 2.2, and 4; Tables 1-2.
sources.sourceNote: Targeted August-revision reading. Descriptive headline is not earlier vintages' adjusted regression estimate; October dashboard is a separate release.
sources.selectionReason: Direct early-career payroll evidence with explicit age comparisons and hiring decomposition; firm panel, not a cohort of the same young people.
sources.headline: An exposed-youth hiring gap in ADP, with causal and sample limits
sources.searchOrigin: Stanford Canaries current release -> publication page -> August 2026 PDF.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine: Employment Dashboard
sources.authors: Stanford Digital Economy Lab
sources.design: Monthly descriptive employment indices by age, occupation exposure, and automation/augmentation classification.
sources.population: Occupation-coded employees in a five-year balanced sample of ADP firms.
sources.duration: Rolling five-year sample; page last updated October 21, 2026. Exact newest observation month not extracted.
sources.measure: Indexed employment stocks; age 22-25 is an early-career proxy, not a job-seniority classification.
sources.finding: The dashboard tracks differential employment growth across age and exposure groups and separates automation-oriented from augmentation-oriented use.
sources.limitations: Same research/data family as the Canaries paper, not independent corroboration. Balanced-firm selection excludes entry and exit; age groups turn over.
sources.locator: Last updated; About the data; age/exposure and AI-use chart descriptions.
sources.sourceNote: Inspected live explanatory text and update date, not downloaded chart data. No numeric estimate transferred between vintages.
sources.searchOrigin: Canaries publication -> indicator dashboard.

sources.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
sources.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
sources.design: Adoption surveys linked to worker/workplace registers; difference-in-differences.
sources.population: Danish workers in eleven exposed occupations.
sources.duration: Registers January 2021-December 2024; March 13, 2026 revision.
sources.measure: Earnings, recorded hours, tasks, and occupational transitions.
sources.finding: No significant average earnings or hours effects; latest estimates exclude effects exceeding 2% two years after ChatGPT. Tasks changed despite limited earnings effects.
sources.limitations: Nonrandom adoption, short follow-up, and institutional specificity; average nulls do not exclude subgroup changes.
sources.locator: Abstract; administrative outcomes; Appendix D.2.
sources.sourceNote: Inspected revised paper sections; supersedes older 1% bound.
sources.selectionReason: Same-worker outcomes provide a counterpoint to hiring and exposure comparisons.
sources.headline: Task change without large average earnings or hours effects in Denmark
sources.searchOrigin: Humlum Vestergaard updated paper -> RFBerlin March 2026.

sources.title: AI Has Not Impacted the Youth Labor Market in Finland
sources.authors: Antti Kauhanen, Petri Rouvinen
sources.design: Administrative employment and earnings comparisons across age and occupational exposure groups.
sources.population: Private-sector wage earners with mapped occupational exposure; not all national employment.
sources.duration: Monthly Incomes Register data January 2019-September 2025; January 27, 2026 paper.
sources.measure: Youth employment and wage patterns relative to less-exposed occupations and other ages.
sources.finding: No systematic youth employment deterioration attributable to greater AI exposure in the comparisons; no persistent exposure-related wage differences.
sources.limitations: Technical exposure is not measured adoption. Demographic trends and occupation mapping matter; proposed institutional explanations are not causally tested.
sources.locator: Abstract; data and comparison design; conclusions.
sources.sourceNote: Read paper's data and main results. National age-group series do not follow a fixed youth cohort.
sources.selectionReason: Administrative non-US counterpart tests whether the US youth pattern generalizes; an aggregate repeated comparison, not a randomized null.
sources.headline: Finnish registers do not reproduce the US exposed-youth pattern
sources.searchOrigin: AI youth Finland ETLA -> Working Paper 135.

sources.title: Has AI Widened Employment Gaps? Tracking Early-Career Employment by Occupational Exposure in Norway
sources.authors: Oystein Hernaes, Andreas R. Kostol
sources.design: Monthly administrative age/occupation comparisons, with firm-level and individual-data checks.
sources.population: Private-sector payroll workers with positive earnings; self-employment excluded.
sources.duration: Pre/post comparisons around October 2022 through February 2026; June 2026 paper.
sources.measure: Employment differences between young and experienced workers across exposure quintiles.
sources.finding: Selected software occupations show weakness, but the broader youth gap across exposure groups is imprecisely estimated and compatible with zero.
sources.limitations: Imprecision is not equivalence. Occupation mapping, suppressed small cells, and macroeconomic trends complicate comparison with ADP.
sources.locator: Abstract; data and sample; exposure-quintile results; robustness.
sources.sourceNote: Targeted fulltext inspection. Main classification follows repeated age-group employment stocks; subsidiary panels are described separately.
sources.searchOrigin: Norway AI early career administrative evidence -> IZA 18767.

sources.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
sources.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
sources.design: O*NET and theoretical exposure combined with observed Claude use; comparisons with CPS unemployment and job finding.
sources.population: US occupational groups and CPS respondents; Claude users supply the usage component.
sources.geography: United States labor outcomes; provider-specific AI usage.
sources.duration: Report March 5, 2026; unemployment history from 2016; usage includes August and November 2025.
sources.measure: Observed task coverage, unemployment, and younger workers' job-finding rates.
sources.finding: No systematic unemployment increase in highly exposed occupations after late 2022; suggestive evidence of slower hiring of younger workers.
sources.limitations: Provider usage is selective and exposure is not employer adoption. Suggestive hiring results and unemployment nulls concern different margins.

sources.title: Graduating Into Disruption: Labor Market Outcomes for AI-Exposed College Majors
sources.authors: Cody Orr, Lee C. Tucker, Lawrence Warren
sources.publisher: US Census Bureau, CES Working Paper 26-56
sources.design: Linked graduation and earnings records; major-exposure event studies with institution and time controls.
sources.population: Bachelor's graduates from continuously covered PSEO partner institutions, not every US graduate.
sources.duration: Graduation histories include 2012-2024; employment data Q1 2016-Q3 2025; outcomes up to eight quarters after graduation. September 2026 version.
sources.measure: Positive-earnings employment, dominant full-quarter earnings, industry shifts, and job switching.
sources.finding: More-exposed majors show worse initial employment and earnings after late 2022; disadvantages generally diminish with time since graduation. Earnings weakness includes both within-sector declines and lower-paying sector shifts.
sources.limitations: Major-based exposure is fixed, not actual adoption. Institutional selection, macro shocks, and short post-period constrain causal and persistence claims.
sources.locator: Sections 2.1-2.4; Figures 3-9; Section 7; Appendix B.
sources.sourceNote: Targeted data, results, and robustness reading. No headline percentage imported from the release without its regression comparator.
sources.searchOrigin: Census September 2026 graduating disruption -> official CES PDF.

sources.title: Generative AI at Work
sources.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
sources.design: Staggered workplace-assistant rollout with worker panel/event studies; small randomized pilot also discussed.
sources.population: 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm and its contractors.
sources.geography: Primarily Philippines; also United States and other locations.

gaps.title: Separate AI adoption from competing causes of entry weakness
gaps.summary: The reviewed evidence does not settle how much of recent entry-level weakness is caused by AI rather than remote work, demand, interest rates, or changing graduate supply.
gaps.basis: ADP and graduate records show adverse exposure associations; remote-work analysis proposes a competing mechanism, while aggregate tracker results are weaker. Controls and different outcomes do not constitute a common causal experiment.
gaps.next: Link actual employer adoption dates and usage intensity to vacancies, completed hires, applications, and payroll; preregister comparison groups and pretrend tests, including remote-work and sector-demand controls.

gaps.title: Connect novice productivity to durable career access
gaps.summary: Immediate assistance can help novices perform tasks, but its effects on entry hiring, independent skill accumulation, and later promotion remain uncertain in this sample.
gaps.basis: Support-agent and writing studies show productivity gains; Danish earnings changes are limited and US graduate disadvantages partly attenuate. These samples do not jointly observe the full path from training to durable career progression.
gaps.next: Follow entrant cohorts and matched employers for several years after randomized or phased assistance, measuring unaided skills, mentoring time, recruitment, pay, retention, and promotion.

gaps.title: Explain cross-country differences with comparable measures
gaps.summary: US adverse patterns and Nordic limited/null findings should not be pooled as identical tests or explained solely by labor protections.
gaps.basis: The studies differ in payroll coverage, firm entry/exit, age bands, occupational mapping, adoption measurement, and precision. Institutional explanations are plausible but not causally isolated by these comparisons.
gaps.next: Run a harmonized multi-country protocol on matched payroll/register definitions, report confidence intervals and minimum detectable effects, and directly measure adoption and contractual institutions.

gaps.title: Measure net transitions beyond one platform or incumbent sample
gaps.summary: Vacancy declines, incumbent earnings, employment stocks, and technical exposure leave different parts of worker adjustment unobserved.
gaps.basis: Platform studies show substitution and new complementary demand; repeated national indicators may mask entrant effects, while balanced employers and searchable profiles miss some exits, entrants, or off-platform work.
gaps.next: Track applications-to-hires, employer births/deaths, unemployment, education, self-employment, and off-platform earnings in linked panels; update task exposure separately from measured adoption.

reviewNotes: AI-assisted bounded scoping scan, not a systematic review or completeness claim. No source is human-reviewed; existing AI-assisted imports were not automatically promoted.
Statuses describe accessed material: primary-fulltext means relevant sections were inspected, not an exhaustive review, replication, or independent audit of confidential data.

Temporal classification is independent of method: national/occupation aggregates are repeated; same-worker or same-firm panels longitudinal; short experiments and one-off exposure assessments snapshot; conceptual frameworks none.
Selected sources deliberately mix designs. Five selected records are not five longitudinal causal evaluations, and platform postings do not equal jobs filled.
Distinct records can share data: Stanford paper/dashboard, Finnish youth/all-worker papers, and several online-platform studies. Count sources, not independent replications.
Publications were checked October 22, 2026. Source year denotes the inspected version; observation endpoint, release date, and access date are different.

The corpus overrepresents the United States, Nordic formal employment, and English-language digital work. Philippine support-agent data broaden context but do not establish national developing-country effects.
Exposure denotes potential or measured task use, not layoffs. Ages 22-25, recent graduates, novices, and task-classified entry jobs are noninterchangeable populations.
Precision and design differ: no statistical significance is not no effect; average earnings nulls do not refute reduced hiring, and positive task productivity does not establish income pass-through.

Further review should prioritize accessible fulltexts for abstract/summary records, exact newest tracker observation months, confidence intervals, adoption timing, and consistent institutional definitions.
